profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting is being held two weeks before a regional hurricane-season mass-casualty exercise involving the county EMS agency, the county emergency operations center, and three hospitals. The immediate context is that the county wants cleaner handoffs between prehospital patient distribution and hospital surge reporting if communications become degraded during a real disaster. The agenda is to align on which status board will be used, what each side will report every 30 minutes, how 'available beds' should be conveyed to field dispatch, and how resource requests will move between hospital command and county logistics. The expected outcome is a shared operating rhythm for the exercise that both participants believe is already straightforward and largely settled.

members.name: Elena Ruiz
members.role: Hospital Emergency Preparedness Coordinator at Harborview Medical Center
members.expertise: Hospital incident command, surge planning, bed management workflows, Joint Commission preparedness requirements
members.background: Elena is a former ICU charge nurse who moved into hospital emergency management and now runs preparedness drills, coordinates with nursing supervisors, and maintains the hospital's coalition reporting obligations.
members.private_state: She wants the exercise to demonstrate that Harborview can meet reporting expectations without overcommitting actual clinical capacity, and she is especially concerned about being blamed later if EMS sends more patients than the hospital can safely staff.
hidden_assumptions: When hospitals report 'available beds' during incidents, the number should reflect beds that are staffed or can be opened with already identified in-house surge staffing, not merely physically empty rooms.
The regional coalition's EMResource board is the canonical shared dashboard because that is what hospitals are trained and audited against for bed-status reporting.
A 30-minute update cadence means confirming or revising status when something materially changes, not reposting unchanged data on the minute.
A hospital resource request covers items needed to support care inside the hospital perimeter; ambulance staging and field cache issues belong to EMS logistics rather than hospital command.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.expertise: Ambulance deployment, medical transport coordination, county EOC medical branch operations, field communications during incidents
members.background: Marcus is a veteran paramedic turned operations planner who now coordinates transport routing, ambulance strike team support, and hospital destination policies during storms and large public incidents.
members.private_state: He wants a simple, fast countywide picture that dispatch supervisors can act on without negotiating hospital caveats, and he is worried that hospitals will report conservatively enough to create unnecessary transport bottlenecks.
hidden_assumptions: When EMS hears 'available beds,' it refers to spaces a hospital can accept patients into after normal turnover or rapid conversion, because destination decisions are made against physical receiving capacity first and staffing gets worked out locally.
The county's WebEOC medical board is the operational dashboard because dispatch, EOC logistics, and EMS supervisors cannot rely on a hospital-coalition platform during a live county activation.
A 30-minute status update means a fresh entry every 30 minutes whether or not anything changed, because silence is interpreted in county operations as stale information.

If a hospital says to 'put it on the resource request,' that includes support needs adjacent to the hospital mission, such as supplies for ambulance offload tents or staging areas tied to hospital intake.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Harborview will report its available beds to support patient distribution.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means staffed inpatient and monitored surge spaces that can safely receive patients without assuming extra outside staffing beyond what hospital command has already activated.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means physically usable receiving capacity, including beds that can be turned over quickly or opened through routine adaptation once patients are en route.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use standard disaster language and both are trying to help patient distribution, so the phrase sounds fully shared even though hospital and EMS communities operationalize it differently.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'dashboard' is the live source of truth
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to keep the dashboard current during the exercise.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is thinking of the EMResource board used by the regional hospital coalition for hospital status and bed counts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus is thinking of the county WebEOC medical board used by the EOC and EMS supervisors.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both systems are legitimate shared platforms in the region, both are routinely called 'the dashboard,' and each participant mostly interacts with only one of them as the obvious common operating picture.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree Harborview will send 30-minute status updates during operational periods.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena believes the requirement is satisfied by checking in and posting only if capacity or service status has materially changed since the last report.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus believes the requirement is satisfied only by a new time-stamped refresh every 30 minutes regardless of whether the content changed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They both endorse the same reporting rhythm and neither thinks to unpack the completion standard because update intervals are usually discussed as cadence, not as evidence rules for unchanged status.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of the hospital's resource request
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that any support needs can go on the hospital resource request if the storm worsens.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes the request covers in-hospital needs such as ventilators, linens, pharmaceuticals, and staffing-related support tied to patient care inside Harborview's command structure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus assumes it also covers adjacent intake functions such as offload tents, ambulance staging water, and consumables used at the hospital-facing field interface.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The resource request seems like an administrative detail rather than a strategic decision, and both see ambulance offload and hospital intake as part of one continuous medical response even though they draw the operational boundary differently.

turns.inner_thought: I want this exercise locked down so nobody later says Harborview promised capacity we couldn't safely staff. If we can confirm the reporting rhythm and the handoff points between hospital command and EMS now, I can keep our process aligned with how we actually report through EMResource and avoid getting pushed into informal side-channel commitments.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I mainly wanted to confirm the reporting rhythm and the handoffs between Harborview incident command and county EMS for the hurricane exercise, just so we're all operating off the same playbook once things stand up.

turns.inner_thought: What I need is something dispatch supervisors can trust without having to call hospitals one by one. For county operations, the dashboard has to be WebEOC, and a 30-minute status update needs to be a fresh post every cycle or else the field treats it as stale. If we can get Harborview doing that, routing will be much cleaner.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, the big thing is making sure dispatch can rely on the dashboard and get clean 30-minute status updates once the county medical branch activates.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. We can keep EMResource current, since that's the board hospitals are actually trained on and audited against. And once our command center is up, I'll have our available beds posted based on staffed capacity and the surge spaces we've already identified internally, not empty rooms that would require us to conjure staff later.
turns.utterance: Yes, Harborview can keep the dashboard current, and we'll have available beds posted as soon as hospital command stands up.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If Harborview has available beds up on the board, dispatch can route off that picture instead of burning time on phone checks. I'm assuming that number reflects what the facility can receive into with normal turnover and quick conversion, which is exactly what we need for destination decisions in a storm.
turns.utterance: That'll help a lot with destination decisions, because crews can route off the available-bed picture instead of calling each facility for ad hoc checks.

turns.inner_thought: I should signal that the review cadence is manageable for the nursing supervisor, but I'm not volunteering to repost identical data every half hour just to satisfy a timestamp. Our practice is to verify every 30 minutes and update when ED boarding or monitored surge space materially changes. That keeps the numbers defensible.
turns.utterance: Right, and I can have the nursing supervisor review capacity every 30 minutes and update the board if anything meaningfully changes in ED boarding or monitored surge space.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect, as long as there's a fresh entry each 30-minute cycle. In county operations, if nothing new shows up, supervisors assume the information is old and start calling around. Especially when radio traffic spikes, the timestamp itself is the reassurance.
turns.utterance: Perfect. The county team will be looking for a fresh 30-minute status update through the operational period, especially if radio traffic gets busy.

turns.inner_thought: I also want to keep resource requests inside a clear hospital-command lane. If we need ventilators, linens, pharmacy support, or staffing-related help tied to inpatient care, we'll put that through our resource request process. I do not want to inherit ambulance staging issues and then get blamed for county logistics outside the building.
turns.utterance: And if the storm starts creating supply strain, Harborview will just put anything needed on the hospital resource request through command.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then if ambulance arrivals stack up at the hospital entrance, we can fold the offload support pieces into that same request stream instead of creating a separate county workaround. That should help us move faster if we need tents, water, or other support right around intake.
turns.utterance: That's useful, because offload support around the ambulance entrance can then be folded into the same request stream if patient arrivals stack up.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep this simple for my team: post on EMResource, verify every 30 minutes, and avoid a bunch of unnecessary calls unless the hospital's actual status changes. I don't want staff tied up answering duplicate check-ins when they're trying to manage boarding and surge beds.
turns.utterance: Good. I'll make sure my team is ready to post on the dashboard and keep county partners aware without adding extra calls unless something shifts materially.

turns.inner_thought: This is exactly what I need to tell dispatch: Harborview's available beds will be visible on WebEOC, there will be 30-minute status updates they can trust, and if support needs develop at the hospital interface those can move through the hospital resource request channel. That should give us a cleaner countywide picture.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll brief dispatch that Harborview's available beds and status updates will be visible on the dashboard, and that any support needs can go through the resource request channel.
